title: Lie Algebra Cohomology and Kostants Nilradical Theorem

items.title: Chevalley–Eilenberg cohomology computes Ext of the trivial module
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]); it supplies the Axiom of
Dependent Choice through [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]].
Let $\mathfrak a$ be a Lie algebra over a field $k$ and $V$ an $\mathfrak a$-module,
regarded as a left $U(\mathfrak a)$-module by
[[thm-lie-algebra-representations-are-equivalent-to-unital-modules-over-the-enveloping-algebra]],
and regard $k$ as the trivial module. Then for every $n\ge0$ there is a natural
isomorphism
$$H^n(\mathfrak a,V)\cong\operatorname{Ext}^n_{U(\mathfrak a)}(k,V),$$
where the left-hand side is the Chevalley–Eilenberg cohomology of
[[def-lie-algebra-cohomology]] and the right-hand side is the balanced Ext
bifunctor of [[def-balanced-ext-bifunctor]] computed using supplied projective
and injective resolution data on the objects being compared. Indeed with $P_q=U(\mathfrak a)\otimes_k\Lambda^q\mathfrak a$,
with the module structure induced by the $(U(\mathfrak a),k)$-bimodule structure
of $U(\mathfrak a)$ and with the Koszul differential displayed in step 1.2, the
augmented complex $P_\bullet\to k$ is a resolution of $k$ by free
$U(\mathfrak a)$-modules, evaluation identifies
$\operatorname{Hom}_{U(\mathfrak a)}(P_q,V)$ with $C^q(\mathfrak a,V)$ of
[[def-chevalley-eilenberg-cochains]], and the induced differential is exactly
the zero-based differential of [[def-chevalley-eilenberg-differential]]; hence
the comparison corollary
[[cor-ext-can-be-computed-from-any-projective-resolution-of-the-first-variable]]
computes $\operatorname{Ext}^n$ from this resolution with no new sign
convention.

references.title: Pavel Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, MIT 18.755 lecture notes (Spring 2024), §45.2 pp.246–249 and §48.1 pp.259–261
references.locator: §45.2, printed pp.247–249, the trivial-coefficient Chevalley–Eilenberg complex; §48.1, printed p.260, cochains with coefficients. The standard free resolution is proved locally, not in these passages

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.2 printed pp.64–70
references.locator: §3.2.2, printed p.69, derived invariants and the Ext identification; the arbitrary-field standard resolution is constructed locally

items.strategy: Exhibit the Koszul/standard free resolution of the trivial module; identify its Hom-complex with the published Chevalley–Eilenberg complex on the nose; invoke the independence-of-resolution corollary for the balanced Ext bifunctor. Dependent Choice enters only through the comparison of supplied resolution data.

items.title: Degree-zero Lie algebra cohomology is the invariant subspace
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak a$ be a Lie algebra and $V$ an $\mathfrak a$-module. In the
convention of [[def-chevalley-eilenberg-cochains]], evaluation at $1$ identifies
$C^0(\mathfrak a,V)$ with $V$, and [[def-chevalley-eilenberg-differential]] gives
$(d^0v)(x)=x\cdot v$ for $x\in\mathfrak a$, $v\in V$. Hence
$$H^0(\mathfrak a,V)=V^{\mathfrak a}=\{v\in V:x\cdot v=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathfrak a\},$$
so the degree-zero cohomology is the invariant subspace; for the trivial module
this reads $H^0(\mathfrak a,k)=k$. This normalizes the degree-zero end of the
page and agrees with [[prop-zero-th-lie-algebra-cohomology-is-invariants]].

references.title: Pavel Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, MIT 18.755 lecture notes (Spring 2024), §45.2 pp.246–249 and §48.1 pp.259–261
references.locator: §48.1, printed p.260, the degree-zero identity H^0(g,V)=V^g

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7

items.strategy: Read off $d^0v=x\cdot v$ from the published differential; $H^0=\ker d^0$ because $C^{-1}=0$, and the kernel is the invariants. A convention check against the published DG-29 statement, not a new argument.

items.title: The normalizer acts on Lie algebra cohomology
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak a$ be an ideal of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak p$ and let $V$ be a
$\mathfrak p$-module, restricted to $\mathfrak a$. This covers
$\mathfrak a=\mathfrak n^+\triangleleft\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$
and, with $\mathfrak p=N_{\mathfrak g}(\mathfrak a)$ the normalizer of
[[def-normalizer-of-a-lie-subalgebra]], every subalgebra whose normalizer is to
act. For $x\in\mathfrak p$ define the Lie derivative on cochains by
$$(\theta_x\omega)(x_1,\dots,x_q)=x\cdot\omega(x_1,\dots,x_q)-\sum_{j=1}^q\omega(x_1,\dots,[x,x_j],\dots,x_q),\qquad \omega\in C^q(\mathfrak a,V),$$
and for $x\in\mathfrak a$ let $i_x:C^q(\mathfrak a,V)\to C^{q-1}(\mathfrak a,V)$
be the contraction $(i_x\omega)(x_1,\dots,x_{q-1})=\omega(x,x_1,\dots,x_{q-1})$.
Then $\theta$ is a representation of $\mathfrak p$ on $C^\bullet(\mathfrak a,V)$,
each $\theta_x$ commutes with the differential $d$ of
[[def-chevalley-eilenberg-differential]], and for $x\in\mathfrak a$ one has
$\theta_x=di_x+i_xd$ (Cartan's formula), so $\theta_x$ acts as zero on
cohomology. Consequently $\theta$ descends to a representation of the quotient
Lie algebra $\mathfrak p/\mathfrak a$ on $H^\bullet(\mathfrak a,V)$, making it a
$U(\mathfrak p/\mathfrak a)$-module; in particular $H^\bullet(\mathfrak n^+,V)$
is an $\mathfrak h$-module for every $\mathfrak b$-module or $\mathfrak g$-module
$V$.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.2 printed pp.64–70
references.locator: §3.2.3, printed p.69, Lie derivative for an ideal and Proposition 3.2.7 on the quotient action; Cartan identities in §3.2.1, pp.65–68

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed pp.1–2, cochains and derived invariants as background; the normalizer and Cartan identities are proved locally, not in these notes

items.strategy: Verify the representation axiom for $\theta$ from the Jacobi identity, $d\theta_x=\theta_xd$ by the standard Cartan computation in the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex, and $\theta_x=di_x+i_xd$ for $x\in\mathfrak a$; the homotopy formula gives triviality on cohomology and the descent to $\mathfrak p/\mathfrak a$.

items.title: Central actions on nilradical cohomology factor through the Harish–Chandra projection
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and triangular decomposition $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak n^-\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$ ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]]), and let $V$ be a $U(\mathfrak g)$-module. Write $\operatorname{pr}$ for the Harish–Chandra projection of [[def-harish-chandra-projection]]. Then for every $z\in Z(U(\mathfrak g))$, every $p\ge0$ and every $\omega\in H^p(\mathfrak n^+,V)$,
$$z\cdot\omega=\operatorname{pr}(z)\cdot\omega,$$
where the left side multiplies cochain values by $z$ and the right side is the $\mathfrak h$-action of [[prop-a-normalizer-acts-on-lie-algebra-cohomology]] applied to $\operatorname{pr}(z)\in U(\mathfrak h)=S(\mathfrak h)$. Thus the $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$-action on $H^\bullet(\mathfrak n^+,V)$ factors through the unshifted projection $\operatorname{pr}$; the $\rho$-shift appears only when $\operatorname{pr}$ is composed with the evaluation that produces the Harish–Chandra isomorphism [[thm-harish-chandra-isomorphism-for-the-center]]. Only the unshifted identity is asserted.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.2 printed pp.64–70
references.locator: §3.2.4–§3.3, printed pp.70–72, Proposition 3.2.9, Propositions 3.2.10–3.2.11, and Theorem 3.3.1 with its dimension-shifting proof

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, discussion of the Casselman–Osborne lemma; no proof is supplied there

items.strategy: Degree zero: $z-\operatorname{pr}(z)\in U(\mathfrak g)\mathfrak n^+$ by the PBW decomposition defining $\operatorname{pr}$, so $(z-\operatorname{pr}(z))v=0$ on $V^{\mathfrak n^+}$. For $p>0$, embed $V$ in an injective $U(\mathfrak g)$-module $I$; since $U(\mathfrak g)$ is free over $U(\mathfrak n^+)$ by PBW, $I$ is injective over $U(\mathfrak n^+)$, so $H^q(\mathfrak n^+,I)=0$ for $q>0$ by the Ext identification and vanishing of positive Ext on injectives. The connecting maps of the long exact sequence are $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$- and $U(\mathfrak h)$-linear, so induction on $p$ through $H^{p-1}(\mathfrak n^+,I/V)\to H^p(\mathfrak n^+,V)$ propagates the identity.

items.title: The Casselman–Osborne constraint on weights of nilradical cohomology
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, positive system
$\Phi^+$, $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\mathfrak g_\alpha$,
$\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ dominant integral, and $V=L(\lambda)$ the
finite-dimensional irreducible module of highest weight $\lambda$
([[thm-highest-weight-classification-of-finite-dimensional-irreducible-representations]]).
If $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ is an $\mathfrak h$-weight of $H^p(\mathfrak n^+,V)$
for some $p\ge0$, then $\chi_\mu=\chi_\lambda$, where
$\chi_\nu\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ is the central character
$z\mapsto\nu(\operatorname{pr}(z))$ attached to the highest weight $\nu$.
Equivalently,
$$\mu\in W\cdot\lambda=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho:w\in W\}$$
by [[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]. This constrains every degree
independently of the harmonic computation below.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.3 printed pp.71–73
references.locator: §3.3, printed p.72, Theorem 3.3.1 on the central action; §3.4, printed p.76, proof of Theorem 3.4.1 deriving equality of central characters and dot-orbit membership

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, Theorem 1 and discussion of the central-action approach; the weight constraint is derived locally

items.strategy: $V$ is irreducible, so each $z\in Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ acts on $V$ by the scalar $\chi_\lambda(z)$ ([[lem-central-action-on-a-cyclic-highest-weight-module-is-scalar]]). On a cohomology weight vector of weight $\mu$, the previous lemma makes $z$ act by $\operatorname{pr}(z)$, and the $\mathfrak h$-action makes $\operatorname{pr}(z)$ act by the scalar $\mu(\operatorname{pr}(z))=\chi_\mu(z)$. Hence $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$; [[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]] converts equality of central characters into membership in the dot orbit.

items.title: The inversion set of a Weyl group element
items.statement:
Let $\Phi$ be a reduced crystallographic root system with positive system
$\Phi^+$ and Weyl group $W$. The standing conventions are those of
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]] and
[[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]: $\Phi^+$ is the positive
system attached to a chamber, each $w\in W$ permutes $\Phi$ and acts on the
ambient Euclidean space, and $\ell$ is the length function of
[[def-length-and-longest-element-of-a-finite-weyl-group]], which is also the
minimal word length in simple reflections
([[prop-weyl-length-equals-positive-root-inversion-number]]). The Lie-algebraic
realization of the same Weyl action is the one of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]] inside
[[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]]. Throughout,
$\rho$ denotes the Weyl vector of [[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]].

**The inversion set.** For $w\in W$ put

$$\Phi_w=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w^{-1}\alpha<0\}.$$

This is the set that indexes the exterior root covectors of the extremal
cochains constructed from this page. It is computed from the inverse action,
not from the action of $w$ itself.

**Identification with the published inversion sets.** The published inversion
set of [[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]],
written $N(w)$ in [[def-length-and-longest-element-of-a-finite-weyl-group]], is
$$\operatorname{Inv}(w)=N(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\},$$
that is, the positive roots sent by $w$ itself to negative roots. With this
convention
$$\Phi_w=\operatorname{Inv}(w^{-1})=N(w^{-1}),$$
since $w^{-1}\alpha\in\Phi^-$ says exactly that $\alpha$ is a positive root sent
by $w^{-1}$ to a negative root. Consequently, by the identification of length
with inversion number and the equality of the lengths of inverse elements,
$$|\Phi_w|=|\operatorname{Inv}(w^{-1})|=\ell(w^{-1})=\ell(w).$$
The middle equality is the definition $\ell(v)=|N(v)|$ of
[[def-length-and-longest-element-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]; the last equality
holds because reversing an expression of $w$ in simple reflections expresses
$w^{-1}$ with the same number of letters, so the minimal word lengths agree,
and both equal the inversion numbers
([[prop-weyl-length-equals-positive-root-inversion-number]];
[[lem-finite-weyl-strong-exchange-and-deletion]], which states that word
length equals inversion length for these simple reflections).

**Extremal values and the half-sum identity.** For the unit $1\in W$ nothing is
inverted, $\Phi_1=\varnothing$; for the longest element $w_0$, whose existence
and uniqueness are proved in
[[prop-weyl-length-equals-positive-root-inversion-number]] and which satisfies
$w_0(\Phi^+)=\Phi^-$, one has $w_0^{-1}(\Phi^+)=\Phi^-$ and hence
$\Phi_{w_0}=\Phi^+$. Moreover
$$\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\alpha=\rho-w\rho .$$
Indeed, $w\Phi^+=\{\beta\in\Phi:w^{-1}\beta\in\Phi^+\}$, and this set is the
disjoint union of the positive roots with $w^{-1}\alpha>0$ and the negatives of
the roots in $\Phi_w$: a root $\beta$ with $w^{-1}\beta>0$ is either positive,
or of the form $-\alpha$ with $\alpha\in\Phi_w$, and no other possibility
occurs. Since $\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$ and
$w\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\beta\in w\Phi^+}\beta$, the difference is
$$\rho-w\rho=\tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha-\sum_{\alpha:w^{-1}\alpha>0}\alpha+\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\alpha\Bigr)=\tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\alpha+\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\alpha\Bigr)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\alpha .$$
The first sum is over all positive roots, the second over the positive roots
with $w^{-1}\alpha>0$, and their difference is the sum over $\Phi_w$. This
identity is the sign-normalized half-sum statement used, in the form
$\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\alpha=\rho-w\rho$, in the extremal-cochain lemma below.

references.title: Roe Goodman and Nolan Wallach, Symmetry, Representations, and Invariants, GTM 255, Appendix E: Cohomology and Character Formulas, §E.2.1–§E.2.6, printed pp.17–30

items.strategy: Identify $\Phi_w$ with the published inversion set $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\beta>0:w^{-1}\beta<0\}$; length equality is the published strong-exchange statement. The half-sum identity follows by splitting $\Phi^+$ into $\{\alpha:w^{-1}\alpha>0\}$ and $\Phi_w$: $\rho-w\rho=\frac12\sum_{w^{-1}\alpha>0}\alpha-\frac12\sum_{\Phi_w}\alpha=\sum_{\Phi_w}\alpha$.

items.title: The extremal weight cochain of a Weyl element is closed and unique
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex semisimple with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, Weyl group $W$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ dominant integral and $V=L(\lambda)$. For each $\alpha\in\Phi^+$ fix a nonzero covector $\varepsilon_\alpha\in(\mathfrak n^+)^*_{-\alpha}$ annihilating $\bigoplus_{\beta\neq\alpha}\mathfrak g_\beta$, for each $w\in W$ fix a nonzero $v_{w\lambda}\in V_{w\lambda}$, and let $\Phi_w$ be the inversion set of [[def-inversion-set-of-a-weyl-group-element]] with $p=\ell(w)=|\Phi_w|$. Then
$$\gamma_w=\Bigl(\bigwedge_{\alpha\in\Phi_w}\varepsilon_\alpha\Bigr)\otimes v_{w\lambda}\in C^{p}(\mathfrak n^+,V)$$
is a nonzero cocycle of weight $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$, and the cochain weight space at $w\cdot\lambda$ is one-dimensional in exactly that degree:
$$C^q(\mathfrak n^+,V)_{w\cdot\lambda}=0\ (q\neq\ell(w)),\qquad C^{\ell(w)}(\mathfrak n^+,V)_{w\cdot\lambda}=\mathbb C\gamma_w .$$
Consequently $[\gamma_w]\neq0$ spans the one-dimensional space $H^{\ell(w)}(\mathfrak n^+,V)_{w\cdot\lambda}$, and its one-dimensional cohomology line depends only on $w$ and not on the choices of $\varepsilon_\alpha$, $v_{w\lambda}$ or the ordering.

Equality case (Kostant's lemma): if $\eta$ is a weight of $V$, $S\subseteq\Phi^+$ and $\mu=\eta-\sum_{\alpha\in S}\alpha$ satisfies $\|\mu+\rho\|=\|\lambda+\rho\|$ in the form on $\mathfrak h^*$ induced by the Killing form, then there is a unique $w\in W$ with $\mu=w\cdot\lambda$, $S=\Phi_w$ and $\eta=w\lambda$.

items.strategy:
Cochain weights are of the form $\mu=\eta-\sum_{\alpha\in S}\alpha$ with $\eta$ a weight of $V$, $S\subseteq\Phi^+$. If $\mu=w\cdot\lambda$ then $\eta+ho-\sum_S\alpha=w(\lambda+ho)$; choose $u$ with $
u=u(\mu+ho)$ dominant. Since $\lambda+ho$ is strictly dominant and $w(\lambda+ho)$ is a $W$-translate, the unique dominant translate forces $
u=\lambda+ho$ and $u=w^{-1}$. Write $u\eta=\lambda- eta$ ([[lem-highest-weight-modules-have-weights-below-the-top-weight]]) and $u(ho-\sum_S\alpha)=ho-\sum_T\alpha$ by induction on a reduced word for $u$ using the signed permutation of positive roots; then $\|\lambda+ho\|^2-\|
u\|^2=(\lambda+ho+
u, eta+\sum_T\alpha)$, which is nonnegative and vanishes only for $ eta=0$, $T=\varnothing$. Hence $\eta=w\lambda$ and $\sum_S\alpha=ho-who=\sum_{\Phi_w}\alpha$; if $S
eq\Phi_w$ the symmetric difference is nonempty and each leftover root $\eta'$ satisfies $(who,\eta')>0$, so $(who,\sum_S\alpha-\sum_{\Phi_w}\alpha)>0$, contradicting equality of the sums. Thus $S=\Phi_w$; multiplicity one follows from $\dim V_{w\lambda}=1$ and the one-dimensionality of the root covectors. Finally $d\gamma_w\in C^{p+1}_{w\cdot\lambda}=0$ and $C^{p-1}_{w\cdot\lambda}=0$, giving closedness and nontriviality.

items.title: The Chevalley–Eilenberg Laplacian is scalar on weight components
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex semisimple with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, Killing form $B$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ and $V=L(\lambda)$. Choose a compact real form of $\mathfrak g$ with conjugation $\tau$ and root vectors normalized by $B(e_\alpha,f_\alpha)=1$, $f_\alpha=-\tau(e_\alpha)$; give $\mathfrak n^+$ the Hermitian form $\langle x,y\rangle=-B(x,\tau y)$ and $V$ a positive Hermitian form invariant under the compact real form. Such a compact form and form exist by [[thm-compact-connected-semisimple-lie-groups-are-classified-up-to-isogeny-by-root-systems]], [[thm-compact-connected-lie-groups-are-classified-by-root-data]] and [[thm-lie-second-fundamental-theorem]], and the representation is unitarizable by [[thm-every-finite-dimensional-continuous-representation-of-a-compact-lie-group-is-unitarizable]]; let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ also denote the induced tensor form on $C^q=\Lambda^q(\mathfrak n^+)^*\otimes V$. Let $d$ be the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential [[def-chevalley-eilenberg-differential]], let $\delta=d^*$ and $\square=d\delta+\delta d$. Write $d=A+D$ with $A=\sum_{\alpha>0}\varepsilon_\alpha\pi(e_\alpha)$ and $D=-\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}c^\gamma_{\alpha\beta}\varepsilon_\alpha\varepsilon_\beta\iota_\gamma$ for the structure constants $[e_\alpha,e_\beta]=\sum_\gamma c^\gamma_{\alpha\beta}e_\gamma$, and set $T(H)=-\sum_{\alpha>0}\alpha(H)N_\alpha$, $N_\alpha=\varepsilon_\alpha\iota_\alpha$, $\Theta(H)=\pi(H)+T(H)$. Then:
(i) $\langle\square c,c\rangle=\|dc\|^2+\|\delta c\|^2\ge0$ for all $c$, with equality exactly on $\ker\square$; hence $C^q=\operatorname{im}d\oplus\ker\square\oplus\operatorname{im}\delta$ and harmonic representatives identify $H^q(\mathfrak n^+,V)\cong\ker\square\cap C^q$;
(ii) $\{D,D^*\}=-\frac12\sum_jT(H_j)^2-T(H_\rho)$ and $\{A,A^*\}+\{A,D^*\}+\{D,A^*\}=\sum_{\alpha>0}\pi(f_\alpha)\pi(e_\alpha)-\sum_j\pi(H_j)T(H_j)$ for a $B$-orthonormal basis $H_j$ of the real Cartan span;
(iii) with the polarized Casimir form of [[def-quadratic-casimir-element]] and [[prop-the-quadratic-casimir-element-is-central]],
$$2\square=1\otimes\pi(C_{\mathfrak g})-\sum_j\Theta(H_j)^2-2\Theta(H_\rho),$$
so on every weight component $C^\bullet_\mu$ actually occurring in the finite cochain space,
$$\square|_{C^\bullet_\mu}=\tfrac12\bigl(\|\lambda+\rho\|^2-\|\mu+\rho\|^2\bigr)\operatorname{id},$$
the norm coming from $B$. The scalar is nonnegative, and it vanishes exactly when $\mu\in W\cdot\lambda$ lies in the dot orbit. The normalization of $B$, of $C_{\mathfrak g}$ and of the root-vector metric is common and fixed once and for all; rescaling one of them independently changes the scalar.

items.strategy:
Step 3 local calculation with the Killing-form normalization. Unitarize the compact-form action; then $\pi(e_a)^*=\pi(f_a)$, the $\varepsilon_a$ are orthonormal for the dual metric, and distinct cochain weights are orthogonal. DG-29's differential gives $A=\sum_a\varepsilon_a\pi(e_a)$ and $D=-\frac12\sum_{a,b,c}c_{ab}^c\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_b\iota_c$. Since the Hermitian product is linear in its first argument, $A^*=\sum_a\pi(f_a)\iota_a$ and $D^*=-\frac12\sum_{a,b,c}\overline{c_{ab}^c}\varepsilon_c\iota_b\iota_a$.

The CAR relation gives $\{A,A^*\}=\sum_a\pi(f_a)\pi(e_a)+\sum_{a,b}\varepsilon_a\iota_b\pi([e_a,f_b])$, $\{A,D^*\}=-\sum_{a,b,c}\overline{c_{ab}^c}\varepsilon_c\iota_b\pi(e_a)$, and $\{D,A^*\}=\sum_{a,b,c}c_{ab}^c\varepsilon_a\iota_c\pi(f_b)$; degree-four terms cancel in the last two expressions. Compact conjugation and $B$-invariance give $[e_\alpha,f_\beta]=-\overline{c_{\beta\gamma}^\alpha}e_\gamma$ if $\alpha=\beta+\gamma$, $[e_\alpha,f_\beta]=-c_{\alpha\gamma}^\beta f_\gamma$ if $\beta=\alpha+\gamma$, and $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=H_\alpha$. The off-diagonal terms cancel termwise against $\{A,D^*\}$ and $\{D,A^*\}$; the diagonal sum is $\sum_\alpha N_\alpha\pi(H_\alpha)=-\sum_j\pi(H_j)T(H_j)$.

For the exterior anticommutator, CAR normal ordering cancels degree-six terms and gives $\{D,D^*\}=\frac12\sum_{p,q,r}|c_{pq}^r|^2N_r+\sum_{a<b,\,c<d}K_{ab;cd}\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_b\iota_c\iota_d$, where $K_{ab;cd}=-\sum_s c_{ab}^s\overline{c_{cd}^s}-\sum_s\overline{c_{sc}^a}c_{sb}^d+\sum_s\overline{c_{sc}^b}c_{sa}^d+\sum_s\overline{c_{sd}^a}c_{sb}^c-\sum_s\overline{c_{sd}^b}c_{sa}^c$. Put $X_{ac}=[e_a,f_c]=X_{ac}^++X_{ac}^0+X_{ac}^-$, where $X_{ac}^+=\sum_{s>0:\,a=s+c}\overline{c_{sc}^a}e_s$, $X_{ac}^0=\mathbf1_{a=c}H_a$, and $X_{ac}^-=-\sum_{s>0:\,c=a+s}c_{as}^c f_s$. Thus $[e_b,f_c]=\mathbf1_{b=c}H_b+\sum_s\overline{c_{sc}^b}e_s-\sum_sc_{bs}^c f_s$, and compact conjugation gives $[f_c,f_d]=-\sum_s\overline{c_{cd}^s}f_s$. Set $S(X,Y)=B(X^+,Y^-)+B(Y^+,X^-)$. Then $K_{ab;cd}=J_{ab;cd}-S(X_{ac},X_{bd})+S(X_{ad},X_{bc})$, where $J_{ab;cd}=-\sum_s c_{ab}^s\overline{c_{cd}^s}=B([e_a,e_b],[f_c,f_d])$. Jacobi, paired with $f_d$ and using invariance, gives $J_{ab;cd}=B(X_{ac},X_{bd})-B(X_{ad},X_{bc})$. Since $B(X,Y)=S(X,Y)+B(X^0,Y^0)$, the root terms cancel and $K_{ab;cd}=B(X_{ac}^0,X_{bd}^0)-B(X_{ad}^0,X_{bc}^0)=(a,b)(\mathbf1_{a=c}\mathbf1_{b=d}-\mathbf1_{a=d}\mathbf1_{b=c})$. Thus the quartic part is $-\sum_{a<b}(a,b)N_aN_b$.

For the linear coefficient, take $E=\operatorname{ad}e_r$, $F=\operatorname{ad}f_r$. On $\mathfrak n^+$, $\operatorname{tr}[E,F]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}H_r)=\sum_{\beta>0}(\beta,r)=2(\rho,r)$. The $e_r$ term contributes $\|r\|^2$; each raising root string cancels between $EF$ and $FE$; each unordered decomposition $r=a+b$ contributes $2|c_{ab}^r|^2$. Hence $\frac12\sum_{a,b}|c_{ab}^r|^2=(\rho,r)-\frac12\|r\|^2$, yielding $\{D,D^*\}=-\frac12\sum_jT(H_j)^2-T(H_\rho)$. Combining with the mixed identity and $C_{\mathfrak g}=\sum_jH_j^2+2H_\rho+2\sum_{a>0}f_ae_a$ gives $2\square=1\otimes\pi(C_{\mathfrak g})-\sum_j\Theta(H_j)^2-2\Theta(H_\rho)$. Since $\pi(C_{\mathfrak g})$ acts on $L(\lambda)$ by $\|\lambda+\rho\|^2-\|\rho\|^2$ and $\Theta(H)$ acts on cochain weight $\mu$ by $\mu(H)$, $\square$ is $\frac12(\|\lambda+\rho\|^2-\|\mu+\rho\|^2)$ on every weight component actually occurring in the finite cochain space. The zero set follows from the equality case in the extremal-cochain item. The cited sources prove the cohomological Casimir identity, not the cochain identity. Step 3 authorship must write out the CAR normal ordering and root-string trace terms in the item proof; no Jacobi coefficient cancellation remains unproved.

items.title: Each extremal harmonic space is one-dimensional
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the setting of
[[lem-kostant-laplacian-is-scalar-on-weight-components]], for every degree
$q\ge0$ the harmonic cochains are spanned by the extremal cochains of the Weyl
elements of length $q$:
$$\ker\square\cap C^q(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\bigoplus_{w\in W:\,\ell(w)=q}\mathbb C\gamma_w,$$
where $\gamma_w$ is the cocycle of
[[lem-extremal-weight-cochain-for-a-weyl-element-is-closed]]. Each summand is
one-dimensional, so $\dim(\ker\square\cap C^q)=\#\{w:\ell(w)=q\}$, and the
harmonic projection gives $H^q(\mathfrak n^+,V)\cong\ker\square\cap C^q$. In
particular the zero eigenspace of $\square$ is exactly the span of the
$\gamma_w$, with one line per element of $W$.

references.title: Roe Goodman and Nolan Wallach, Symmetry, Representations, and Invariants, GTM 255, Appendix E: Cohomology and Character Formulas, §E.2.1–§E.2.6, printed pp.17–30
references.locator: §E.2.4–§E.2.5, printed pp.24–27, Lemma E.2.8, Theorem E.2.9, equation (E.44), and Corollary E.2.10; the harmonic interpretation is supplied by the local Laplacian lemma

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.4 printed pp.73–77
references.locator: §3.4, printed pp.73–76, Lemmas 3.4.3–3.4.5 and Remark 3.4.6(i)

items.strategy: The Laplacian is scalar on each weight component, by the previous lemma, and vanishes exactly on the dot-orbit components. The cochain multiplicity statement of the extremal-cochain lemma says that in degree $q$ the dot-orbit weight $w\cdot\lambda$ occurs only for $\ell(w)=q$, with one-dimensional space $\mathbb C\gamma_w$. Summing over $w$ gives the displayed direct sum; Hodge decomposition from the previous lemma gives the identification with $H^q$.

items.title: Kostant's nilradical cohomology theorem
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ and $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, and let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ be dominant integral with $V=L(\lambda)$. Then for every $k\ge0$ there is an isomorphism of $\mathfrak h$-modules
$$H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)\cong\bigoplus_{w\in W:\,\ell(w)=k}\mathbb C_{w\cdot\lambda},$$
where $\mathbb C_\mu$ is the one-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-module of weight $\mu$ and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Equivalently, $H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)$ is multiplicity free with weights exactly the pairwise distinct weights $w\cdot\lambda$ over the length-$k$ elements, and $\dim H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\#\{w\in W:\ell(w)=k\}$.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.4 printed pp.73–77
references.locator: §3.4, printed p.73, Theorem 3.4.1 (Kostant) with Remark 3.4.2; printed p.76, Remark 3.4.6(i) on the dimension count

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, Theorem 1 for finite-dimensional irreducible highest-weight coefficients

items.strategy: The harmonic projection is an $\mathfrak h$-linear isomorphism $H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)\cong\ker\square\cap C^k$; the extremal-harmonic lemma identifies the right side with $\bigoplus_{\ell(w)=k}\mathbb C\gamma_w$, where $\gamma_w$ has weight $w\cdot\lambda$. The weights $w\cdot\lambda$ are pairwise distinct because $\lambda+\rho$ is regular ([[lem-positive-root-pairings-of-a-dominant-integral-weight]]).

items.title: Kostant cohomology in degrees zero and top
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the setting of [[thm-kostant-nilradical-cohomology-theorem]]:
$$H^0(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\mathbb C_\lambda$$
is the highest-weight line, i.e. the $\mathfrak n^+$-invariants; $H^{|\Phi^+|}(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\mathbb C_{w_0\cdot\lambda}$ for the longest element $w_0\in W$ ([[prop-weyl-length-equals-positive-root-inversion-number]]); and $H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)=0$ for $k>|\Phi^+|$. When $\Phi^+=\varnothing$, $\mathfrak n^+=0$ and $H^0(\mathfrak n^+,k)=k$ with all higher cohomology zero.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.4 printed pp.73–77
references.locator: §3.4, printed pp.73 and 76–77, Remark 3.4.2 (H^0 is the highest-weight space) and Remark 3.4.6(i)

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, Theorem 1, specialized locally to the endpoint lengths

items.strategy: Degree zero: $W_0=\{1\}$ and $1\cdot\lambda=\lambda$, so the theorem gives the highest-weight line; independently $\mathfrak n^+$-invariants are highest-weight vectors. Top degree: the only element of length $|\Phi^+|$ is $w_0$. All degrees above $|\Phi^+|$ have no Weyl elements and vanish. The rank-zero case is the empty positive system.

items.title: The Kostant Euler character recovers the Weyl numerator
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the setting of [[thm-kostant-nilradical-cohomology-theorem]], define the formal character of a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-module by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu\dim(M_\mu)e^\mu$. Then
$$\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\operatorname{ch}H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\cdot\lambda}.$$
The right-hand side is the finite alternating character computed directly from Kostant's decomposition. The separate BGG/Weyl-character identity at [[cor-bgg-euler-character-identity]] identifies this same finite sum as the Weyl numerator. Thus the cohomological computation of the sum itself does not use Weyl-character input; its interpretation as the numerator is the comparison supplied by that identity.

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed pp.6–7, Euler–Poincaré argument and the alternating cohomology character

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.5 printed pp.77–84
references.locator: §3.5.2, printed pp.82–84, the cohomological recovery of the Weyl character formula numerator

items.strategy: Substitute the multiplicity-free weight list of the Kostant theorem into the alternating sum of formal characters; each weight $w\cdot\lambda$ occurs exactly once, in degree $\ell(w)$. This proves the displayed identity directly from the cohomology decomposition. The separate BGG/Weyl-character identity is only the comparison that names the finite sum as the Weyl numerator; it is not used in the computation.

items.title: Kostant cohomology and BGG characters give the same Weyl numerator
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$. Put
$D=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})$ and
$N_\lambda=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\cdot\lambda}$. In the Grothendieck
group of the linkage block $\mathcal O_\lambda$, the BGG resolution gives
$[L(\lambda)]=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}[M(w\cdot\lambda)]$ by
[[thm-bgg-resolution-of-a-finite-dimensional-simple-module]]. Applying its
formal-character map and the Verma character formula
[[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]] gives
$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=D^{-1}N_\lambda$. Separately, the spaces
$H^k(\mathfrak n^+,L(\lambda))$ are finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-modules,
and [[thm-kostant-nilradical-cohomology-theorem]] gives
$\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\operatorname{ch}_{\mathfrak h}H^k(\mathfrak n^+,L(\lambda))=N_\lambda$,
as recorded in
[[cor-kostant-euler-character-recovers-the-weyl-numerator]]. Thus the
character calculations identify the same finite Weyl numerator after clearing
the Verma denominator in the BGG character formula. No equality between classes
in different Grothendieck groups is asserted, and no spectral sequence is
constructed.

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed pp.6–7, the cohomological Weyl numerator; the BGG comparison is supplied by the cited library items

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.5 printed pp.77–84
references.locator: §3.5.2, printed pp.82–84, the cohomological proof of the Weyl character formula

items.strategy: First take the alternating class of the finite BGG resolution in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ and apply its formal-character map; substitute the Verma character formula to obtain $D^{-1}N_\lambda$. Separately sum the one-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-characters in Kostant's cohomology decomposition to obtain $N_\lambda$. Compare these expressions in the common formal-character completion after clearing $D$. Keep the two Grothendieck-group contexts distinct; do not treat the $\mathfrak h$-modules as objects of the Category-$\mathcal O$ block.

title: Lie Algebra Cohomology and Kostants Nilradical Theorem — Examples

items.title: Kostant cohomology for sl2
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from Kostant's theorem ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$, with Cartan subalgebra
$\mathfrak h=\mathbb C H$, positive root $\alpha$, Weyl vector
$\rho=\alpha/2$, fundamental weight $\omega=\alpha/2$, and $\lambda=m\omega$
with $m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, so that $V=L(m\omega)$ has dimension $m+1$ and
$\mathfrak n^+=\mathbb C e_\alpha$. The Weyl group is $\{1,s\}$ with
$s\cdot\lambda=s(\lambda+\rho)-\rho=-\lambda-2\rho=-(m+2)\omega$. Kostant's
theorem gives
$$H^0(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\mathbb C_{m\omega},\qquad H^1(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\mathbb C_{-(m+2)\omega},\qquad H^k(\mathfrak n^+,V)=0\ (k\ge2),$$
with generators $v_{m\omega}$ and $\varepsilon_\alpha\otimes v_{s\lambda}$,
where $v_{s\lambda}\in V_{s\lambda}$ has weight $s\lambda=-m\omega$. This
verifies the sign of the dot action, the $\rho$-shift and the top degree in the
smallest rank, and shows that the degree-one weight is $-(m+2)\omega$, not
$-m\omega$.

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, Theorem 1, specialized locally to sl2; the cochain weights are computed here

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.4 printed pp.73–77
references.locator: §3.4, printed pp.73–77, the rank-one specialization of Theorem 3.4.1

items.strategy: Specialize the two corollaries to rank one: $W=\{1,s\}$, $\ell(s)=1$, $\dim\mathfrak n^+=1$, and compute $s\cdot\lambda=-(m+2)\omega$ directly.

items.title: Kostant cohomology for the trivial sl3 module
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from Kostant's theorem ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3(\mathbb C)$, $\lambda=0$ and $V=\mathbb C$ the trivial module. Here $W\cong S_3$ has elements $1,s_1,s_2,s_1s_2,s_2s_1,w_0$ of lengths $0,1,1,2,2,3$, and the dot action is $w\cdot0=w\rho-\rho$. Kostant's theorem therefore gives
$$H^k(\mathfrak n^+,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{\ell(w)=k}\mathbb C_{w\cdot0},$$
of dimensions $1,2,2,1$ in degrees $k=0,1,2,3$ with pairwise distinct weights $0,-\alpha_1,-\alpha_2,-2\alpha_1-\alpha_2,-\alpha_1-2\alpha_2,-2\alpha_1-2\alpha_2$; in particular $\dim H^1(\mathfrak n^+,\mathbb C)=2$, one class for each simple reflection, and the total dimension is $|W|=6$. This is the first rank-two check of the multiplicity-free formula, and it shows that a trivial coefficient module does not force all cohomology weights to vanish.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.4 printed pp.73–77
references.locator: §3.4, printed pp.73–76, Theorem 3.4.1 and Remark 3.4.6(i), specialized locally to trivial sl3 coefficients

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, Theorem 1, specialized locally to the trivial sl3 module; no rank-two cohomology calculation is given there

items.strategy: Identify the sl3 roots as A2; enumerate the six Weyl elements and their lengths, evaluate w dot 0=w rho-rho for each element, then apply Kostant to obtain dimensions 1,2,2,1 and the six distinct weights.

items.title: Degree-one Kostant classes correspond to simple reflections
items.statement:
In the setting of [[thm-kostant-nilradical-cohomology-theorem]],
$$H^1(\mathfrak n^+,V)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\mathbb C_{s_i\cdot\lambda},$$
one line for each simple reflection $s_i$, generated by the classes of the
extremal cochains $\gamma_{s_i}$ of
[[lem-extremal-weight-cochain-for-a-weyl-element-is-closed]]. This identifies
the common simple-reflection indexing of degree-one Kostant cohomology and the first term
$\bigoplus_iM(s_i\cdot\lambda)$ of the BGG resolution, without identifying the cohomology lines with the Verma modules, and shows that distinct
simple roots give distinct weights, because $\lambda+\rho$ is regular.

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.4 printed pp.73–77
references.locator: §3.4, printed pp.73–77, Theorem 3.4.1, Lemma 3.4.5 and Remark 3.4.6(ii) on the degree-one cocycles

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed p.4, Theorem 1 and discussion of extremal cochains and the BGG approach; the simple-reflection indexing is derived locally

items.strategy: Degree-one elements of $W$ are exactly the simple reflections; apply the theorem and the explicit cocycle construction. Distinctness of the weights follows from regularity of $\lambda+\rho$.

items.title: Whitehead vanishing does not apply to the nilpotent radical
items.statement: **False claim.** The semisimplicity hypothesis of the Whitehead lemmas can be replaced by nilpotency of the coefficient Lie algebra: for every finite-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebra $\mathfrak a$ over a field of characteristic zero and every finite-dimensional $\mathfrak a$-module $M$, one has $H^1(\mathfrak a,M)=0$.

references.title: Peter Woit, Lie Algebra Cohomology and the Borel–Weil–Bott Theorem (Math G4344, Spring 2012), printed pp.1–7
references.locator: printed pp.1–2, cochains and invariants as background; the one-dimensional nilpotent counterexample is computed locally

references.title: Faisal Al-Faisal, On the Representation Theory of Semisimple Lie Groups (University of Waterloo MMath thesis, 2010), §3.2 printed pp.64–70
references.locator: §3.2, printed pp.64–68, the cochain complex and the degree-one computation

items.strategy: Direct computation in degrees zero and one: $[\mathfrak n^+,\mathfrak n^+]=0$ makes all 1-cochains closed and $d^0=0$ makes none exact; compare with the semisimple Whitehead hypotheses and with the rank-one case of the theorem.

items.title: Omitting the exterior root-weight shifts gives the wrong dot weight
items.statement: **False claim.** The weight of the degree-one Kostant generator for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ can be computed without the exterior root-weight contribution: taking only the extremal vector gives the weight $w\lambda=-m\omega$, and attaching the $\rho$-shift to the top weight gives the weight $\lambda-\alpha=(m-2)\omega$. In particular the exterior factor $\varepsilon_\alpha$ may be dropped from the generator, or the whole $\rho$-shift counted only once off the exterior part.

references.title: Direct sl2 cochain-weight check against the sign conventions of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex; this ai-generated row is not a dependency target for any item
references.locator: direct rank-one computation

items.strategy: Compare the three displayed weights in rank one; $s\rho=-\rho$ gives $s\rho-\rho=-2\rho=-\alpha$, and $s\cdot\lambda=-\lambda-2\rho$, so the listed alternatives are off by $2\omega$ and by $2m\omega$ respectively.
